articles.title: US inequality is getting worse in ways you might not expect
articles.author: Markus Schneider, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Denver
paras: The buzzword of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections may be affordability, but growing anger over inequality is behind the sentiment.

A Pew Research survey released in October 2026 found that roughly 6 in 10 Americans – including 4 in 10 Republicans – believe there’s too much inequality in the U.S. And a growing share from both major political parties state that the economy needs to be fundamentally rebuilt to address this.

This sentiment has, however, been difficult to convert into political results. Public support for California’s proposed wealth tax on billionaires has been waning ahead of the midterms, for example, and in 2025, Republicans passed President Donald Trump’s sweeping legislation that included tax cuts for the wealthy while cutting safety net programs.

I’m an economist who has been studying inequality for about two decades. My research confirms the trend of rising inequality since 1980, driven by the wealthiest pulling away not just from the middle class, but also from the “merely wealthy.” Overall, recent research underscores how policy choices – including taxation and public spending – enabled this 40-year rise in inequality.

Some policies enacted more recently appear to be accelerating this trend. An analysis by the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, a nonpartisan research organization, concluded that policy changes since the start of 2025 have imposed higher costs on everyone except the top 1%.

Recent federal data shows that wealth inequality continues to grow. The top 1% saw their share of wealth increase from 31.7% to 32.5% just between the first and second quarters of 2026, a jump of over $8.5 trillion. That caps a steady climb from 30.9% in the last quarter of 2024 – and from 27.4% in 1999.

These recent gains come at the expense of the middle class – the 40% between the bottom half and the top 10% – who hold only 28.8% of all wealth despite being a group that’s 40 times larger than the top 1%. And the middle’s share is shrinking, down from 32.9% in 1999 and 30.2% at the end of 2024, according to the data.

But the ultra-wealthy, those in the top 0.1%, are pulling away even from the rest of the rich, the data shows. This tiny elite owns 15% of all wealth – almost half of all the wealth of the top 1%. Both the top 0.1% and the next 0.9% saw their share of wealth increase, but the top 0.1% captured two-thirds of the gains between the first and second quarters of 2026.
Even within the highest echelons of wealth concentration, these two groups are on different trajectories.

Crucially, the wealth of the top 0.1% is disproportionately boosted by corporate profits, which are up sharply overall. The top 0.1% reap the most from this growth because their portfolios’ value has soared on the promise of future increased profitability that’s driving up stock prices – especially thanks to the tech and artificial intelligence boom.
Since President Ronald Reagan’s tax cuts in the 1980s, the U.S. tax code has become less and less progressive, often through policy changes supported by both Republicans and Democrats.

The common argument for tax cuts is that they stimulate growth, but a growing body of research – including international studies – doesn’t back that up. A 2025 Brookings report notes that U.S. tax policy has gone through massive changes throughout history without any discernible effect on growth.

Nonetheless, congressional Republicans used their narrow majorities in 2025 to pass Trump’s sweeping policy and tax bill, which included provisions making most of his 2017 tax cuts permanent. Those included the historically low top-income tax rate and the lowest corporate tax rate since 1940.

It’s also important to understand that the top 0.1% have a different tax exposure from the rest of the top 1% because the composition of their wealth is different. They own as much in stocks and mutual funds as the next 0.9%, a group that is nine times larger, and those holdings are where most of their recent gains came from.

Furthermore, roughly three-quarters of the top 0.1%’s wealth portfolio consists of corporate and business ownership, allowing them to benefit from the Trump tax cuts in multiple ways – including lower tax rates and more opportunities to defer or avoid tax liability. Their massive holdings of stock mean that they can borrow against it for cash, usually tax-free, rather than having to sell shares.

By contrast, below that elite, real estate is a much more important component of wealth, while corporate equity is a smaller and smaller share. For the middle class, nearly two-thirds of wealth is held in their homes and retirement savings, while corporate and business ownership accounts for only 15%.
The new drivers of inequality

Much of the inequality debate focuses on the role that taxation has played. But other recent policy changes have shifted different kinds of costs on to low- and middle-income earners, while leaving the wealthy relatively unscathed.

One example is a provision in Trump’s 2025 legislation that allowed federal healthcare subsidies through the Affordable Car Act to lapse. Insurers and analysts expect the number of people signing up for coverage through ACA plans to drop by about 5 million due to higher premiums and face much higher out-of-pocket costs.

The spike in energy costs, including gasoline, diesel and heating oil, is another case in point. They disproportionately affect low- and middle-income consumers but barely dent the budgets of the wealthy – while boosting the profits of companies engaged to the extraction, processing and transportation of oil. This divergence has been especially pronounced since the start of the conflict with Iran in February 2026, which has pushed up the global price of oil.

Then there are tariffs, which are fundamentally a consumption tax on imports. Economists at the New York Federal Reserve have found that these levies have inflicted a heavy hit on many common consumer goods. They estimated that prices for these items, which make up a much larger share of household budgets among the nonwealthy, would have fallen on average by 1% over the year without the tariffs. Instead, they have risen by 2.9%.

This acceleration in the redistribution of wealth from the middle class to the very top, in short, has an array of drivers. But they’re not inexorable forces of history. As economist Thomas Piketty put it in “A Brief History of Equality,” published in 2022: “Inequality is first of all a social, historical, and political construction.”

articles.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
articles.author: Jordi Calvet-Bademunt, Research Fellow and Visiting Scholar of Political Science, Vanderbilt University
paras: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about 1 in 5 voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found.

But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad.

I’m a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, where I study free speech policy. In two reports published in 2025 and 2026, my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they often use existing rules, such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say.
Censorship masked as safety
AI can cause real harm, from launching cyberattacks to generating sexualized images of children.

It’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to control political discussion, particularly chatbot responses about those in power.

In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google’s Gemini chatbot whether the policies of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, were fascist. Gemini responded that some experts say yes. The government reacted by requiring official permission before “unreliable” AI models could be released. Although authorities later dropped this requirement, the case shows how terms like “under-testing” or “unreliable” can be used for political purposes.
India is not alone. China requires AI models to uphold “socialist core values.”

And in Turkey, a court blocked posts by Grok, the chatbot built into the social platform X, that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. Research by Turkish law scholar Yaman Akdeniz identifies the Turkish rulings as among the earliest documented cases of state censorship of chatbots.

Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court sentenced two activists, who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how prosecutions can target political criticism.
Foreign rules, domestic impact
Some of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders.

The European Union’s AI Act, adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe, wherever it is based, to mark AI-generated content. Anthropic, for one, applies the marks globally because it has no reliable way to apply them by region. This is an example of the Brussels Effect, in which rules adopted in the EU end up applying elsewhere.
European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics.

In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act, Europe’s online safety rulebook. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, now must assess and reduce the “systemic risks” of its service, including risks to elections, such as the spread of disinformation.

And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the political middle ground “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.”
These rules can be used to pressure platforms.

In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, warning against the spread of “harmful content.”
The United States is no exception
Threats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad.

In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.”

“Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently banned three news outlets from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and dismissed media polls as “fake.”
More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that steer answers toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law.

A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts. In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues.

Meanwhile, dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes. California and Hawaii, for example, are two states that have banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election. U.S. courts have blocked both of those laws, citing the First Amendment.

What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box.

Jordi Calvet-Bademunt is affiliated with The Future of Free Speech, a nonpartisan, nonprofit think tank located at Vanderbilt University. The organization is supported by foundations and individual donors, and it retains full independence and final authority over its work, including research, methodology, analysis, conclusions, and presentation.

articles.title: Are partisan politics even changing up our accents? They just might be, y’all
articles.author: Valerie M. Fridland, Professor of Linguistics, University of Nevada, Reno
paras: With the midterms fast approaching, communicating just the right message has been top of mind on all sides of the political aisle.

Whether that message drives home a lack of affordability as gas, food and home prices surge or stokes fears about the rise of communism in the American heartland, Democrats and Republicans are spending a lot of time thinking about what to say.

But as a linguist who studies the impact of accents on the way people are perceived, I believe how politicians and voters say what they say might be just as important as the words they use in understanding the social consequences and linguistic changes resulting from the political divides that are growing between us.

If there is one regional American accent that has long endured on the lips of its speakers – as well as in the minds of listeners beyond the region – it’s the Southern accent. From North Carolina through Texas and pretty much all states in between, the so-called Southern drawl has long been emblematic of a distinct culture found in the South.

Yet, in the urban South, recent linguistic research finds that the drawl’s most salient features are starting to fade on the lips of young speakers. Fewer “pins” are merged with “pens,” and pronunciations such as “far” for “fire” or “say-ud” for “said” are becoming rarer.

While linguists have been busy trying to understand this trend, political scientists have been measuring how different accents perform on the campaign trail. The verdict? Southern accented candidates are generally heard as more conservative than those without a Southern accent, particularly to Democratic listeners.

Putting these findings from linguists and political scientists together, alongside a spate of studies examining correlations between voting patterns and vowels, hints, I believe, that the increasing conservative-liberal divide in American politics just might be the key to understanding what’s driving the decline of the drawl in the urban South.
Out of the mouth of the South

The traditional Southern accent has no shortage of stereotypes: From positive, friendly, country and down-home vibes to negative, backward, uneducated and lazy tropes, the accents of William Faulkner, Bill Clinton and the hillbilly Clampetts have weathered it all.
The reality, of course, is that the Southern accent is not some incorrect version of a national standard but instead a historically separate and unique dialect – or, more accurately, set of dialects.

As explored in my recent book, this dialect formed from linguistic variation that came in with colonial-era settlers from different places and stations. The incipient differences increased after the Civil War intensified hostilities and cultural differences between the North and South.

The association with “countryness” often triggered by a Southern accent grew out of this region’s agricultural past and its related cultural folkways. But what “country” has come to mean relies largely on stereotypes about what a country lifestyle involves. They include things like hunting, gun ownership and less socially progressive views – often arising from media portrayals of and beliefs about the South.

As the South has become more and more industrialized over the past half-century, these social meanings associated with the accent’s use now highlight a disconnect between its new urban vibe and its older, traditional rural one.
As rural vs. urban ideological and political divides in the U.S. have intensified, so has using symbolic means to signal this opposition.

Pickup trucks emblazoned with American flags and country music have become politicized. The white Southern accent, by virtue of its association with more rural traditional values, has also become emblematic of a conservative political identity not all modern Southerners share.

Recent linguistic research has compared voters in the South who had strong Southern accents to those with weaker ones, mainly measured through their use of a set of unique Southern vowel pronunciations, such as saying “bay-ud” for “bed” or “rawed” for “ride.”

It turns out that those holding more right-leaning positions and voting Republican in previous presidential elections used significantly more Southern vowels than those with more left-leaning positions who voted for Democrats. Three separate studies in Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee discovered the same relationship between degree of Southern accent and political conservatism or liberalism.
The takeaway from these studies is that conservatism itself is embodied in a strong Southern accent.
New sound to the urban South?
The pronunciation of one’s vowels has become a barometer of how one’s beliefs and values fit within the old vs. new South.

Conservative ideologies and politics have become enmeshed with “country” speech and lifestyles. Young urban Southerners who don’t identify with these traits might be moving not so much away from Southern identity itself but rather specifically from this rural conservative identity it is often associated with.

Of course, other factors are also playing a role in the decline of the Southern accent in cities, such as heavy migration by non-Southerners to the region and greater interaction with people from other dialect areas via social media.

Outside the South, interestingly, recent research has found a greater embrace of Southern accent features, emerging in particular among those in rural areas where traditional lifestyles and, often, more conservative views are embraced. For instance, in a small, rural town in Ohio, speakers who identified themselves as more drawn to country lifestyles showed use of vowel features – such as saying “baa” for “bye” – more associated with the South.

So, in this circuitous and indirect way, vowels have become the latest players in partisan politics: Democratic Southerners wanting to distance themselves from the ideological and political climate associated with the rural South are moving away from its unique vowels. More “traditional” or conservative-leaning speakers continue to embrace them.

The real casualty in this particular battleground might be the obscuring of a larger culture, practice and community that the Southern accent has long represented for those who are automatically – and often erroneously – assigned a politicized identity just by the sound of their voice.
Valerie M. Fridland has received funding from The National Endowment for the Humanities and the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Are transgender sports bans really about protecting women? Survey data tells a different story
articles.author: Tatishe Nteta, Provost Professor of Political Science, UMass Amherst
paras: Relatively few transgender athletes participate in high school and collegiate sports. Still, since 2020, 27 states have passed laws banning them from participating in sports based on their gender identity.

Just weeks after his second inauguration in 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order prohibiting transgender women and girls from participating in women’s sports in K-12 schools, colleges and universities that receive federal funds. Supporters of these bans often argue that they protect women and girls from unfair or unsafe competition. As Trump said at the signing ceremony: “we will not allow men to beat up, injure and cheat our women and our girls.”

WNBA star Sophie Cunningham offered a similar rationale in a July 2026 ESPN profile: “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

These statements suggest that those in favor of bans are motivated by their admiration for female athletes. But are Americans with more positive views of women and women’s sports more likely to oppose transgender women competing in women’s sports?

We are political scientists who study public opinion toward transgender Americans. To understand how attitudes about gender shape Americans’ views on policies that adversely affect the rights of transgender Americans, we asked 1,000 American adults about their support for restricting the participation of transgender athletes in sports. We also asked about their feelings toward women as a group, their endorsement of sexist stereotypes and their attitudes toward policies that promote gender equity, such as Title IX, the law requiring schools that receive federal funding to provide women and girls with equal opportunities to participate in athletics.
Sexism and support for bans

Our survey found significant public opposition to transgender athletes playing on teams that match their gender identity. When asked whether they “support or oppose a bill that prohibits transgender youth from joining school-sponsored sports teams that match their gender identity,” about half of respondents supported the restriction.

But admiration and support for women do not translate into greater support for excluding transgender people. In fact, individuals with the most negative views of women and gender equality are the most likely to support these bans.

We asked respondents to rate how they feel about women on a scale from 0 to 100. Researchers have used this tool, known as a feeling thermometer, for decades to measure how Americans feel about different groups, including people of color, gay and lesbian people and members of the opposite political party. Among respondents with the most positive views of women, 45% supported restricting transgender sports participation; among those with the most negative views of women, 58% supported restrictions.

We also tested whether more sexist views predicted support for these bans. To measure sexism, we asked respondents how much they agreed or disagreed with three statements about women: “Women seek to gain power by getting control over men,” “Women are too easily offended” and “Women exaggerate problems they have at work.” Social scientists commonly use these questions to measure “hostile sexism,” a set of stereotypes in which women are portrayed as incapable, manipulative and controlling. Among the least sexist respondents, 28% supported banning transgender people from sports matching their gender identity; among the most sexist, 79% did.

If admiration and support for female athletes drive support for prohibiting transgender women from participating in women’s sports, then those who favor Title IX should also favor bans. Instead, 43% of Title IX supporters favored restrictions, compared with 70% of Title IX opponents.

Our findings – that negative attitudes toward women and opposition to Title IX predict support for banning transgender women from sports that match their gender identity – hold even after accounting for other factors like partisanship, ideology and demographic characteristics.

The debate over transgender athletes is often framed as a matter of protecting women. Our findings complicate that narrative: People with the most negative attitudes toward women – and toward policies that protect women’s sports – are the most supportive of banning transgender women from women’s sports.

That does not mean that everyone who supports a ban is motivated by hostility toward women. But the consistency of these findings makes it difficult to accept that protecting women is a primary reason why Americans support these restrictions.

articles.title: Will Reform UK’s racism scandal cost votes? Here’s what previous polling tells us
articles.author: Thomas Lockwood, PhD Researcher in Politics, York St John University
paras: ITV’s newly released documentary Undercover: A Year in Reform has raised fresh questions about Nigel Farage’s party, after covertly recorded footage showed councillors and candidates making racist, Islamophobic, misogynistic and violent remarks. The investigation also exposed the party’s vetting procedures and internal discussions about controversial candidates.

The immediate consequences have included resignations and suspensions of Reform UK councillors and candidates. But whether the documentary’s revelations will translate into lost votes is less certain.

The documentary’s significance lies partly in the questions it raises about organisational responsibility. Reform has said it has improved its vetting procedures since the 2024 general election and insists that there is “no room for racism” in its ranks. Farage, meanwhile, has argued that parties cannot vet people for everything they might say in the future.

The disciplinary position is not uniform. According to ITV’s published account of what has happened to those councillors and candidates featured in the documentary, several have since resigned from their posts or the party, while others remain in place.

Aspiring parliamentary candidate Jason Powell was suspended by Reform after recordings emerged of him advocating the building of concentration camps to house migrants who arrive on small boats. He also said that Muslims cannot be British.
The revelations raise a broader question. Do voters regard the remarks of Reform councillors and candidates as as isolated acts of misconduct, or evidence of a problem with the party itself?
The gap between perceptions and votes

Polling from before the documentary’s release offers a useful starting point. In October 2025, YouGov found that 47% of Britons considered Reform UK generally racist, while 43% said the same of its voters. The same YouGov poll found that 90% of Reform voters considered the party generally not racist, 88% said the same of its policies and 87% considered Reform voters to be generally not racist.

These findings reveal a divide between Reform supporters and the wider electorate. But they don’t establish whether the party’s supporters approve of racist remarks. YouGov research found that 86% of Reform supporters considered immigration a major national issue, while 35–39% cited perceived honesty or the need for political change to be among the party’s attractions. However, polling cannot establish whether these voters would overlook racist remarks in making their voting decisions.

The latest widely reported YouGov poll on voting intention figures, conducted on October 11–12, put Reform at 21%. With the documentary initially being broadcast on October 18, the figures taken before the broadcast provide a baseline for future voting intentions. But it’s not yet clear whether the ITV documentary will now have discouraged people from voting Reform.
What happened when Ukip faced similar scrutiny?
The UK Independent Party’s (Ukip) experience in 2014-15 provides a useful, if imperfect, historical comparison, due to a similar series of controversies involving candidates’ remarks.

William Henwood, a council candidate, tweeted that comedian Lenny Henry should emigrate to “a black country”, prompting his resignation from the party. Andre Lampitt, who appeared in Ukip’s European election broadcast, was suspended after racist and islamaphobic tweets emerged.

Other candidates came under scrutiny for comments about Islam and the murder of Stephen Lawrence, while The Guardian newspaper revealed that one candidate’s Facebook page showed a “like” for a group devoted to the far-right British National Party.
On May 7 2014, Farage rejected accusations that Ukip was racist, arguing that the controversial remarks of a small number of candidates did not represent the party as a whole.

An ITV News/ComRes poll surveying 2,052 British adults the previous month reported that 32% of respondents considered Ukip to be a racist party. Yet among people who said they were likely to vote in the European elections in May, Ukip received the most support with 38% – although its share fell to 32% when a broader group of likely voters was included.
A separate YouGov poll published days later put Ukip on 29% for the European elections.

Together, these polls suggested that concerns about racism can coexist with strong electoral support, but couldn’t establish whether the controversies reduced Ukip’s support. When votes were counted on May 22, the party won 27.5% of the vote in Great Britain and 24 seats in the European parliament.

The polls differed in their timing and methods, and were unable to isolate the effect of the allegations. Nevertheless, they demonstrated that substantial reputational concerns could coexist with strong electoral support. Ukip’s opponents could persuade many people that the party attracted racist candidates – but this didn’t necessarily affect the amount of votes they received. Nor can we tell how Ukip might have performed without the controversies.
The electoral test yet to come
For Reform, any political consequences of revelations about their representatives can’t be inferred from public condemnation alone.

The crucial distinction is between disapproval and defection. Research suggests that voters’ responses to political controversies depend partly on their existing party loyalties and their tolerance of political misconduct. A 2014 study based on British survey data, found that both factors shaped how people judged political controversies.

More recently, a 2026 study found that well-substantiated evidence of misconduct during the Partygate scandal was associated with less favourable evaluations of the governing Conservative Party and reduced voting intentions. Even loyal voters may punish a party when evidence of misconduct is clear.

Neither voter loyalty nor the severity of a controversy alone determine its electoral consequences. Some voters may discount allegations against a party they support, while others may reconsider when evidence is clear and responsibility is apparent. Whether voters prioritise a party’s policies over the conduct of its candidates also cannot be assumed.

Establishing the documentary’s effects on perceptions of Reform’s credibility, or their organisational competence, would require polling that directly measures public reactions as well as subsequent voting intentions. It is too early to conclude that the programme has either damaged Reform electorally, or left its support unchanged.

The central question is not simply whether voters condemn racism, but whether they regard the controversy as important enough to change their political choices. Ukip’s experience shows why that relationship cannot be assumed. For Reform, the longer-term test will be whether voters continue to see these incidents as individual failings, or increasingly associate them with the party’s organisation and leadership.

articles.title: The ‘activity trap’: fear of losing benefits is stopping some disabled people from exercising
articles.author: Toni Williams, Associate Professor, Department of Sport and Exercise Sciences, Durham University
paras: For some people with disabilities, going swimming or attending an exercise class comes with a worry that many others would never consider: could being seen to be physically active lead to their disability benefits being stopped?

This fear is known as the activity trap. A new report published by Disability Rights UK draws on research I led at Durham University and developed with disabled people and disability organisations. Of the disabled people we surveyed, 80% worried that being physically active could put their benefits at risk.

Only one in five participants who had applied for or were receiving benefits were happy with how much physical activity they did. Nearly three-quarters said they would be more likely to increase their activity if they knew their benefits would not be affected.

Disabled people already face barriers to physical activity, including high costs and facilities that are difficult to access. Nearly 40% of disabled adults in England do less than 30 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity a week, according to Sport England. This means activity that makes someone breathe faster than usual, such as brisk walking. The proportion is almost twice that of non-disabled adults.
The activity trap was first highlighted in research published in 2018, when almost half of disabled respondents said they feared losing benefits if they were seen being active.
To explore how this fear affects people’s lives, we surveyed more than 200 disabled people and held group discussions with more than 30 participants. We also examined relevant laws and legal cases.

Participants described feeling encouraged to exercise to manage their health while worrying that being active could be taken as evidence that they no longer needed financial support. One participant said: “I would love to go to the gym, every day, but I don’t dare because I would be seen as being too physically fit.”
Others worried about being reported for benefit fraud if someone saw them enjoying an activity in public.

More than one-quarter of participants who had applied for or were receiving benefits reported having benefits or other financial support removed because of physical activity. These findings describe participants’ experiences; the survey alone cannot establish why individual benefit decisions were made.
How can physical activity affect benefits?

Much of our research focused on personal independence payment (PIP). This benefit helps with the extra costs of living with a disability or long-term health condition. People can receive it whether they work or not.

To decide who qualifies, officials assess how someone’s condition affects everyday activities, such as preparing food, washing and moving around. Going to the gym does not automatically mean someone will lose their benefits. But evidence of physical activity may be considered when deciding what someone can do.

Under existing PIP guidance, assessors must consider whether someone can carry out an activity safely, to a reasonable standard, as often as needed and without taking an unusually long time. They must also consider conditions that vary from day to day.

Yet participants told us that assessors sometimes appeared to place too much emphasis on isolated examples of physical activity, without adequately considering the pain, fatigue or other difficulties they experienced.

Our examination of legal cases revealed similar problems. In one 2024 upper tribunal case, a decision about a man’s entitlement to PIP had relied partly on observations of his ability to walk. However, the tribunal had failed to establish how far he could walk within a reasonable time, how frequently he needed to rest and whether he could repeat the activity. The upper tribunal ruled that the decision was legally flawed and ordered the case to be heard again.

The effects extended beyond physical activity. Of those who answered our survey question about the benefits application process, 84% said it had negatively affected their mental health. Some felt forced to concentrate on everything they could not do, while others said their own accounts or medical evidence were dismissed. The prospect of having to challenge a decision added to their anxiety.
These findings come as the UK government reviews PIP. The Timms review has acknowledged that the current system can discourage physical activity and participation in community life.

Our report calls for better training for assessors, independent advice for people applying for benefits or challenging decisions, and greater involvement of disabled people and organisations led by them in designing the assessment system. These changes could help ensure decisions reflect the realities of living with a disability, including conditions that fluctuate.

A benefits system intended to support the independence of people with disabilities must recognise that occasionally being physically active does not mean someone no longer needs financial support. The challenge now is to ensure that this principle is reflected in how benefits decisions are made.

Toni Williams receives funding from Disability Rights UK. Toni Williams acknowledges the contribution of Sophia Kleanthous, of Disability Rights UK, to the research and the development of this article.

articles.title: Many vapes and e-cigarettes are now banned in Pennsylvania – here’s what Philly consumers and businesses need to know
articles.author: Ana Santos Rutschman, Professor of Law, Villanova University
paras: Many popular nicotine vapes are now banned in Pennsylvania, with only six companies approved to sell their products in the state after a legal ban went into effect on Oct. 19, 2026.
I am a health law professor at Villanova University outside Philadelphia.
Here’s how Pennsylvania’s new law works and what to expect as enforcement begins – especially in Philadelphia, where proximity to states with different laws might pose some challenges.
The products in question include e-cigarettes, vapes and other electronic nicotine delivery systems, commonly known as ENDS.
These products dispense an inhalable aerosol that contains nicotine and other chemicals, including flavoring agents.
ENDS are the most common form of tobacco used by teens and young adults. Flavored vapes are especially appealing to middle and high school students.

In recent years, a growing body of research has studied the health impact of ENDS use, particularly among younger smokers. These studies have raised concerns not only about long-term addiction to nicotine but also exposure to potentially carcinogenic or otherwise harmful chemicals. In 2018, the U.S. surgeon general declared youth vaping an epidemic.

At the federal level, ENDS are regulated by the Food and Drug Administration, but states have the authority to restrict their sale in order to protect the health of their citizens. This is precisely what Pennsylvania has done, joining more than a dozen other states with similar registry laws.
Some popular brands can still be sold

The new law requires the state attorney general to maintain a registry of ENDS approved for sale in Pennsylvania. If a product is not listed in the directory, businesses that sell them will face fines.

The directory currently includes products from just six manufacturers: Juul Labs, R.J. Reynolds Vapor Co., Blue Nine, Custom Technologies, NJoy and Schwartz E-Liquid. However, these manufacturers produce several of the most well-known brands of ENDS, and many of the products included in the directory are extremely popular, such as Juul vaporizers. The reason the new law allows these specific products to continue to be sold is that they have been evaluated by the FDA.

The directory does exclude some very popular products as well, including many brands of disposable vapes and vape juice. The law was designed to specifically ban products that have not been evaluated by the FDA.
If a business sells or offers to sell a product that is not in the directory, the consequences can be severe.

For first-time violations, there will be a fine of up to US$500 per product. A second violation within a year will trigger a fine of $1,000 per day per product until the product is either removed or appears listed in the directory. It will also lead to suspension of the license to sell tobacco products for at least 14 days. A third violation within a year will raise the fine to $1,500 per day per product, coupled with license revocation.

Attorney General David Sunday says his office will focus on “targeted enforcement.” What exactly targeted enforcement means is unclear, but the new law authorizes unannounced inspections. In addition to the premises, inspectors can also examine books and records.
Illegal products that are offered for sale will be subject to seizure and forfeiture, as well as destruction at the business’s expense.
The new law does not impose penalties on consumers who purchase banned products.
What to expect in Philadelphia

Philadelphia was an early adopter of a restrictive approach to the sale of vaping products due to concerns about the youth vaping epidemic. In 2019 the city banned the sale of certain flavored ENDS that were especially popular among adolescent and teen smokers.

Pennsylvania as a whole, however, has been less assertive than some of its neighbors, such as New York, in trying to stop youth vaping. The American Lung Association rates Pennsylvania in the D to F range for its tobacco control policies, below nearby New Jersey, New York and Delaware.

While the Pennsylvania law will reduce the number of products that can be legally sold in the state, it will still be relatively easy for a consumer in Philadelphia to travel to New Jersey or Delaware and buy some of the products banned under Pennsylvania law, including popular brands of disposable vapes.

But additional tobacco control measures may be underway, especially in Philadelphia. On Oct. 15 a member of the Philadelphia City Council introduced a bill that would amend zoning laws in a way that would effectively prevent new businesses selling tobacco and vaping products from opening in many areas of the city.

articles.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
articles.author: Kayla Morton, Assistant Professor of Blue Economy and Policy, University of Delaware
paras: A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate. But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris. It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions, primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient, rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.
Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.
While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts.

Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.
Benefits of federal investment

Elected officials are sometimes accused of “pork barrel politics,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.

Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.”

That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.
The bill’s funding affected the 2024 election
Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election.

During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “economic development opportunities,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself.

Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.

In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.
We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022.

When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.

Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.
These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.

While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections, we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.
Dismantling the subsidies and tax breaks

Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions. A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases.
The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands.

This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.

These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.

articles.title: How candidates are (quietly) talking about climate change – 3 election strategies you’ll see across the US
articles.author: Geoffrey Henderson, Assistant Professor, School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan
paras: Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days. But polls show the majority of voters in 2026 are also concerned about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise.
So why are fewer candidates talking openly about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than just a few years ago?
At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, we study climate communication and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns.

Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to fill up their cars, pay their electric bills and insure their homes against hurricanes and wildfires. It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war.

Fossil fuel industry interests have long sought to polarize the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in his new book, “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change.
When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies.
The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels.

Many have been painting data centers, rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains. Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates. They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to bring their own energy sources onto the grid.

In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S. Senate, emphasizes lowering energy and utility costs. Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “higher electric rates.”

Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that climate change messages can alienate swing voters, who prioritize affordability.

If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both Brown and Cooper have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies.
Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election. However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past.

In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “bold action to invest in clean energy” if reelected in November. In Maine, Senate candidate Troy Jackson asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice.

Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that candidates should link higher costs to climate change, such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk. He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – namely, solar and wind power – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence.

If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change. However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges.
The all-of-the-above proponents

Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways. They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs. Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use cuts against global climate goals.

Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative. These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose “all of the above” energy strategy espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions.

In Iowa, U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled extreme weather is raising insurance costs. But he has also focused on lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel. James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by boosting renewable energy while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources.

These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels. Turek and Talarico are both running in states with abundant wind power.
Where are the voters on this issue?
Studies from the U.S. and Germany find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change.
So how well do candidates’ platforms represent today’s voters?

Yale’s spring 2026 survey found that 49% of voters believe global warming should be a high priority for Congress and the president. But 70% of moderate or conservative Democrats share this view, alongside 84% of liberal Democrats. Even 1 in 3 liberal-to-moderate Republicans considers the climate a high priority.

Yet polling also suggests that other issues, such as the increasing cost of living, are even more important to many voters. This data suggests that pro-climate messages could appeal to swing voters most strongly if climate policies are seen as complementary to affordability.

Still, a recent survey shows that voters open to Democratic candidates are more likely to support a candidate who prioritizes climate change. Climate messaging may especially resonate with young voters. Over a third of those ages 18 to 29 in a recent Harvard Youth Poll considered climate change an urgent national crisis. Young Republicans are more supportive of addressing climate change than their older counterparts.

While many shifts in the way candidates talk about climate policy have little impact on people’s willingness to participate in collective efforts to address it, messages emphasizing cost savings durably increase support for renewable energy across party lines. Voters’ current concerns about inflation could make climate messages involving affordability especially effective in 2026, though the impact of these messages may vary from state to state.
Retail politics and the way forward

These different approaches reflect the Democratic Party’s efforts to build a “big tent” that can attract voters with a wide range of views and priorities. Yet Democrats are generally coalescing around a message designed to appeal to working-class voters: that Trump and the Republicans are raising your cost of living.
November’s midterm elections will offer some insight into whether Democrats’ energy affordability message will resonate in the 2028 presidential election.
Geoffrey Henderson has worked on a project that received funding from the National Science Foundation.
Nathaniel Geiger has received funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Maine Sen. Collins’ success bringing home federal funds is a perfect example of the thin line between political favoritism and effective representation
articles.author: Nicholas Jacobs, Goldfarb Family Distinguished Chair in American Government, Colby College; Institute for Humane Studies
paras: Give politicians the power to decide who gets a government contract, and people will naturally want to get on their good side. After all, the power to hand out something valuable is itself something valuable.

Consider the recent ProPublica investigation involving Sen. Susan Collins of Maine. Martin Kao, the former head of a Hawaii defense contractor called Navatek, told the FBI that his donations to the Republican senator’s campaign and an allied super PAC were part of a deal for help winning federal funding and contracts for his company.
That money padded Navatek’s bottom line, but it was also pitched as an investment in Maine: well-paying jobs from Navy contracts, university research and a new facility on Portland’s harbor.

Trading campaign contributions for official acts, or concealing illegal donations through relatives and shell companies, violate existing law – and it is part of why Kao now sits behind bars. Whether Collins or her official staff knew of an alleged bargain remains a legitimate question the public deserves answered.

But as a scholar of American politics, I argue that the question of criminal corruption obscures a larger problem: The line between political favoritism and effective representation is remarkably thin.
Instead, I wonder why a Hawaii defense contractor concluded that the surest route to federal money ran through a senator from Maine – and why his bet paid off.
Why is access to public money so dependent on the political influence of individual legislators?
The power of appropriators

Earmarks – spending directed by a lawmaker to a specific local project – account for only about 1% of discretionary federal spending, but they offer an unusually clear window into a much larger competition for public money.

Congress revived the practice in 2021, allowing lawmakers to request funding for particular projects in their states and districts. Navatek’s funding came through the Pentagon budget in 2019, when earmarks were banned. But legislative disclosures make it possible to see who asks for money, who gets it and which politicians are best at delivering.
According to Senate Appropriations Committee disclosures, senators submitted 8,071 requests worth US$26.9 billion for fiscal year 2022. By 2026, that grew to 13,997 requests totaling $50.4 billion.
As these requests have grown, however, the share receiving such funding has fallen.

I matched nearly 55,000 Senate requests from fiscal years 2022 through 2026 against the projects Congress ultimately funded. For every senator, I calculated how many projects they requested independently and how many received funding.

The first is the seat: About 30 senators serve on the Appropriations Committee, which writes the bills funding federal agencies. They requested about one-third of the money but secured nearly half of the dollars approved and allocated. A dollar requested by an appropriator was almost twice as likely to become law.

The advantage isn’t partisan: Near the top of the chart, alongside Collins, sit a Vermont Democrat, Patrick Leahy, and a Kansas Republican, Jerry Moran. Leahy retired in 2023, while Moran is still on the panel.

The second is skill: Volume usually costs success – the more a senator asks for, the less of it lands. The median senator won 41% of the money they requested. But Collins is the exception. She requested 496 projects on her own over those five years and won 92% of them – the highest sustained rate in the Senate.

When Republicans regained the Senate majority in 2024, the rate only improved. In fiscal year 2026, her first year as chair, Congress funded 95% of her solo requests, while the median senator’s rate fell to 35%.

When Collins calls her chairmanship a “once in a century” opportunity, she has the evidence. The last Mainer to lead the appropriations committee was GOP Sen. Frederick Hale, who held the chair for four months in the 1930s.

Collins’ chairmanship explains her most recent advantage, but not her entire record. Even before taking the gavel, she secured funding at nearly twice the Senate median. Even in Washington, 30 years of showing up and working across the aisle still gets results.
Forms of political exchange
Now, put yourself in the position of a hospital, a business or a town seeking those dollars. Whose political career would you want to support?

In that respect, Collins is doing what senators are elected to do, and she’s doing it exceptionally well. When access to public resources depends on political influence, those who benefit have reasons to support the politicians most capable of delivering.

Voters call it delivering for Maine. It is why it is a core message of her reelection campaign. You cannot turn on a television in Maine without hearing about some project “Susan” delivered. It has helped get her reelected four times, because people support candidates who promise results; candidates then run on having delivered on that promise.

The same kind of political exchange happens when businesses contribute to super PACs supporting politicians who deliver. It happens when unions organize turnout for candidates promising favorable policies or when nonprofits support politicians who might fund their programs. These are all different forms of political exchange.

Political scientists call this “rent-seeking”: getting ahead by winning government favors rather than creating something of value. And the more government decides who gets what, the harder it becomes to distinguish representation from favoritism.

The Supreme Court confronted this problem in McCormick v. United States, a 1991 case involving campaign contributions and extortion. To violate the law, the court said, payment had to be made in return for explicit, official action.
Otherwise, the court recognized, ordinary campaign finance would become nearly impossible to distinguish from criminal conduct.

The same relationships that make effective representation possible also make political favoritism difficult to distinguish from legitimate government. A company wins a contract after supporting a senator. A nonprofit receives a grant after helping elect an ally.

Even if every senator were ethical, conscientious and committed to the public good, the incentives would remain the same. A senator who refused to compete wouldn’t make their state’s sewers less leaky. They would leave them unfunded while other states secured the money. The problem doesn’t require bad people.
Nor can it be resolved by declaring one set of political interests more virtuous than another.

Collins’ Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, for example, says he isn’t backed by corporate PACs or billionaire donors but by working people. Such a claim implies a distinction between self-interested corporate influence and supposedly public-spirited political support that motivates his donor base – even if that donor base includes a multimillion-dollar “dark money” super PAC.

But when a union invests substantial resources to elect politicians who promise favorable labor legislation, or if a nonprofit mobilizes its members to elect someone who promises to expand grants for its programs, the same client-patron relationship persists.
Corporate entities have particular interests; so do noncorporate entities. Both can expect benefits from government. Patronage exists even when the profits don’t go to shareholders.

To call one form of influence corrupt and the other well intentioned is to paper over the business model of reelection: Have they delivered? Will they continue to deliver? Changing the source of campaign support doesn’t change the powers the winner will exercise.
Restricting earmarks didn’t eliminate the underlying incentives. Nor can campaign finance laws, however necessary, eliminate the value of having a powerful political friend.

If Americans want less rent-seeking, it requires reducing how much government spending depends on discretionary political decisions in the first place. General funding rules, established in advance and responsive to differing local needs, offer one alternative. Such rules wouldn’t remove politics from public spending. But they could shift the political contest away from who gets a particular favor and toward the rules under which everyone receives funding.
Until then, voters face a choice between two kinds of political patrons. Each is asking to hold the pen and write checks. Neither is offering to put it down.

Nicholas Jacobs does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: Young voters fear mass shootings like the one in Oregon, but that fear divides them on gun control
articles.author: Jillian Turanovic, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: A gunman shot and killed three children and a teacher at a school in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15, 2026, the 52nd school shooting this year, according to CNN. The children’s ages were 5, 8 and 11; a 7-year-old and another teacher were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The 16-year-old shooting suspect was shot and killed by a bystander.

Though Oregon has stricter gun laws than most states, some of those laws, such as a measure requiring tougher background checks and requiring a person to have a permit in order to buy a gun, are stalled in court.

The Bend shooting – the latest in a long line of modern school shootings dating back to the late 1980s – comes just weeks before the midterm elections, in which voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws.

Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.

Gun control is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been a recurring part of American life.

Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, at least two students on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at Florida State University. As one of them put it: “This is America.”

Researchers have called today’s young adults the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era, with routine lockdown drills, heightened security in schools and nonstop media coverage of mass violence.

As criminologists who study the impacts of victimization and gun violence among young people, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In a recent study, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.
A debate that repeats after every shooting

Mass shootings account for about 1% of gun deaths in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 survey by the American Psychological Association, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they avoided certain places because of it. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have screening tools to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.

Young adults have also grown up watching the same heated gun debates play out after every tragedy. Gun control advocates call for stricter firearm restrictions to prevent the next mass shooting, whereas gun rights advocates push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase made popular by the National Rifle Association. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses.

Researchers have known for a long time that more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence. A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after decades of mass shootings, federal gun policy has barely budged. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, they’ve faced Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court.

Young people have become some of the loudest voices in this debate, most notably through March for Our Lives – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and other youth-led groups across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among older Americans, many political observers assume stricter gun laws will follow as young people gain voting power.
This fall, voters in a few states will weigh in on gun policy directly.

In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to keep or repeal a 2024 law that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to change the state constitution to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.

So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. Our survey asked young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.

In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.

We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high.

In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the largest voting bloc in the country. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.
This is an updated version of an article originally published on Oct. 15, 2026.
