articles.title: Why the 26 secretary of state races this November matter more than they did before Trump’s drive to assert federal authority over elections
articles.author: Thom Reilly, Professor and Co-Director of the Center for an Independent and Sustainable Democracy, Arizona State University
paras: From Alaska to Florida, there once was an important job in government that most Americans rarely thought about: the secretary of state.

That changed after the 2020 presidential election, when secretaries of state in places such as Arizona, Georgia and Michigan were thrust into battles over election results, certification and false claims of widespread fraud.

In most states, the secretary of state serves as the chief election official, although the precise powers of the office vary. These officials can oversee voter registration, issue guidance to local election administrators, supervise election procedures and, in many states, participate in certifying results.
In the 2022 midterms, some who rejected or sought to overturn the 2020 election ran for these offices across the country.
Of the 13 election-denying candidates for secretary of state who reached the 2022 general election, only three won.

But the struggle over who controls American elections did not disappear. Now, in 2026, it has entered a different phase. It’s a struggle over the constitutionally established power given to states, not the federal government, to run elections. And secretaries of state are key players in this conflict.
Battles over voter rolls, citizenship and federal authority
There are secretary of state contests in 26 states this November.
The United States is unusual in how it selects the officials who administer elections.

Unlike most democracies, many American chief election officials are chosen through explicitly partisan processes, including partisan elections and political appointments. Yet studies have found that Democratic and Republican election officials generally administer elections impartially despite their party affiliations.
These once-obscure offices wield considerable influence.

A secretary of state cannot simply change the result of an election. But depending on state law, the office can have substantial authority over elections before, during and after voting. Secretaries of state may oversee voter registration and voting systems, establish procedures for local election officials, participate in election certification and become involved in disputes over ballot access and election administration.

States United Democracy Center, which describes itself as a “nonpartisan organization advancing free, fair, and secure elections,” defines an “election denier” secretary of state as someone who spread the false claim that Donald Trump won the 2020 election, refused to certify its legitimate results or attempted to overturn them.
The number of secretary of state candidates who deny the legitimacy of the 2020 election has declined since the last midterm, from 13 candidates in 2022 to seven in 2026.
Those declines are notable. But they do not mean disputes over election administration are receding.
Trump administration aims to expand federal election role
U.S. election administration is spread across states, which have primary responsibility for running elections, while Congress can set or alter rules for federal elections.
In practice, state and local officials carry out most of the day-to-day work, including voter registration, operating polling places and counting ballots.
The Trump administration has sought to expand the federal government’s role in several of those areas.

The Justice Department has demanded statewide voter registration lists as part of an effort to identify potentially ineligible registrations. By April 2026, the department said it had sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for failing to provide those records, arguing that the Civil Rights Act of 1960 gives the attorney general authority to obtain and inspect them.

Some states resisted the demands, while others complied. By October 2026, 18 Republican-led states had provided voter information to the federal government. By late summer, federal courts had dismissed DOJ voter list cases against more than 20 states, although appeals remained pending in several of them.
Then, on Oct. 9, 2026, a federal judge went further, striking down the DOJ’s nationwide voter list collection policy itself.

The court ruled that the department lacked authority to collect state voter files, compare them with federal citizenship databases and use those comparisons to press states to remove voters deemed potentially ineligible. The judge concluded that the policy violated federal law and intruded on authority Congress had left with the states.
More federal election initiatives
The administration has gone beyond requesting state voter records.

In March 2025, Trump issued an executive order directing the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of citizenship, such as a passport, from people registering through the federal voter registration form. The administration said the measure was intended to strengthen election integrity and prevent noncitizens from registering or voting.

A federal court permanently blocked that requirement on Oct. 31, 2025, ruling that the president lacked authority to unilaterally change federal election procedures because the Constitution assigns that responsibility to Congress and the states.
The administration has also unsuccessfully pressed Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

Trump issued another election-related executive order in March 2026. It directed the Department of Homeland Security, working with the Social Security Administration, to create state-by-state lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote. It also sought changes in how the Postal Service handles mail and absentee ballots. The White House said the order was designed to enhance election integrity.

In June 2026, a federal court struck down key portions of the order in a lawsuit brought by 23 states and the District of Columbia, blocking its citizenship-list and mail-ballot provisions from taking effect in those jurisdictions during the 2026 elections. In August, however, the Supreme Court stayed that ruling while the litigation continued and did not decide whether the executive order itself was lawful.

The Postal Service later issued a rule requiring states to submit voter information and meet new mail-ballot design and tracking requirements. On Sept. 14, the Supreme Court refused to let the rule take effect for the 2026 elections, leaving a nationwide injunction in place.
Secretary of state races are more consequential now
Collectively, these federal initiatives change the significance of secretary of state races.
Voters in 2026 are choosing state officials who may soon have to decide how their states respond to Washington’s efforts to assert authority over state-run elections.

Should a state provide the federal government with complete voter files containing sensitive information? How should state election officials respond to federally created citizenship databases? What happens when a presidential directive conflicts with state election law – or when courts intervene?
The answers may differ dramatically from state to state.

The officials elected in 2026 will likely be called upon to respond to legal challenges to voter eligibility, election procedures and results, and, in some states, to defend or certify contested outcomes.
For much of American history, that system functioned largely outside the national political spotlight.

The 2026 contests suggest that secretaries of state increasingly stand at the center of a growing conflict over how election authority should be divided between states and the federal government. Who holds these once-obscure offices may therefore matter well beyond the 2026 midterms – and into the 2028 presidential election.

articles.title: Could the UK actually split? Experts explain the legal route for pro-independence leaders
articles.author: Richard Brant, Senior Lecturer in Law, The University of Law
paras: As the Scottish National Party gathered in Aberdeen for the its annual conference, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had also travelled north of the border. SNP conferences are of course a platform for the party to coalesce around its core aim of Scottish independence.

But at Labour’s conference in September, Burnham told colleagues the union is “worth saving” and “worth fighting for” and he was determined not to be “the last prime minister of the United Kingdom”. This was a riposte to SNP leader and Scottish First Minister John Swinney, who had predicted exactly that weeks earlier.

Also in September, Swinney and his fellow pro-independence leaders in Wales and Northern Ireland met for a summit where they asserted their right to decide their own futures. At the talks in Cardiff, the leaders signed two agreements – neither of which changes the law. What they do expose, however, is that the three nations stand in very different legal positions – and that two of them have no route forward at all.

The party leaders (Swinney of the SNP, Rhun ap Iorwerth of Plaid Cymru, and Sinn Féin’s vice president, Michelle O’Neill, and president, Mary Lou McDonald) signed what’s known as a memorandum of understanding.

Officially, the meeting was not a summit of first ministers, rather of party leaders. But this didn’t stop unionists in Northern Ireland criticising O'Neill for taking part while serving as first minister of an executive she leads jointly with deputy first minister Emma Little-Pengelly of the Democratic Uunionist Party. Little-Pengelly is her equal in law.

Swinney and ap Iorwerth also signed a separate pact between their governments – the Cardiff Agreement. It describes the UK in its current form as “unjust and unsustainable” and commits both devolved governments to press for greater powers over their “constitutional future”. Swinney called it an “important moment”. But it is a political statement – in reality, it doesn’t affect either government’s statutory powers.

The two documents speak about self-determination in different registers. The memorandum is bold: it says the three nations have the right to self-determination and no Westminster government has the right to block democracy.

The governments’ agreement is more careful, referring only to the right of citizens to decide their constitutional future “through democratic means”. That difference matters. In international law, the right of peoples to self-determination does not normally give part of a state the right to break away on its own terms, save perhaps in cases of colonial rule or extreme oppression.

The UK Supreme Court said as much in its 2022 ruling, drawing on the Canadian Supreme Court’s decision on Quebec. The claim that Westminster has no right to block these nations’ choices is a political argument, not a statement of the law.
Three nations, three routes

As one of us (Nikos) has argued, only Northern Ireland has a treaty-backed route to exiting the UK. Under the Belfast/Good Friday Agreement and the Northern Ireland Act 1998, the Northern Ireland secretary must call a border poll if it appears likely that a majority would vote for a united Ireland.

Even then, the right belongs to “the people of the island of Ireland”. Reunification needs a majority in Northern Ireland and a separate majority in the Republic, a requirement mirrored in the Irish constitution. The two votes need not fall on the same day, but neither counts without the other.

Scotland’s route is blocked. The power to hold a referendum has to be transferred through a section 30 order, as was the case before the 2014 independence vote. Successive prime ministers have refused, and Burnham’s response to the Cardiff meeting was a statement saying that he “believes strongly in the union … rather than engaging in constitutional debates or further referendums”.
The Scottish government published a draft referendum bill in August, but it will only be introduced once that order is made. While Westminster refuses, the bill is written but unusable.

Wales has an equivalent mechanism – section 109 of the Government of Wales Act 2006. It has never been used to lift the reservation protecting the union of the nations of Wales and England. In September, the Senedd (Welsh parliament) backed a motion asserting Wales’s right to hold a referendum. But a motion settles nothing.

So in two of the three nations, repeated election victories for independence-supporting parties can be followed by an indefinite refusal to organise a referendum. There is no rule to say when that refusal must end.

The Cardiff agreements themselves sit close to a legal line. The Supreme Court has made clear that devolved legislatures cannot use their powers to put pressure on Westminster over the future of the union. Political agreements are not legislation, so they fall outside that test. And signing as party leaders rather than as first ministers adds a further layer of distance.

Legislation is another matter. The Scottish parliament’s 2013 referendum bill succeeded only because the power had already been transferred. That transfer came through a section 30 order in 2013, after the two governments, led by David Cameron and Alex Salmond, settled the terms in Edinburgh.

Cameron agreed because the SNP had won an outright majority at Holyrood (as the parliament is known), which made refusal hard to sustain. The transfer was time-limited: the order required the poll to be held no later than December 31 2014, after which the competence lapsed. The “once in a generation” referendum returned a vote against independence.

Judges at the Supreme Court held unanimously that the 2022 draft, without such a transfer, was outside Holyrood’s competence. The bill was never introduced: the Scottish government’s own senior law officer, the Lord Advocate, put the question to the court first. The problem was not how the bill was drafted but what it was about, and no redrafting could change that. The union between the nations of Scotland and England is reserved to Westminster.

The deeper problem is that the UK has no agreed rules for when a sustained democratic demand obliges the UK government to respond. Canada has developed a duty to negotiate, which would be triggered by a clear majority on a clear question. Until the UK finds its own answer, the question of whether the union is voluntary will keep being asked at the ballot box and refused in Whitehall.

articles.title: Why the GOP’s voter fraud messaging may backfire
articles.author: Christopher Miller, Visiting Assistant Professor of Philosophy, Politics, Economics, and Law (PPEL), University of Richmond
paras: With Election Day 2026 just weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the results will almost certainly hinge on voter turnout, just as they did in 2024.

Given that genuinely undecided voters are scarce — as little as 5% to 7% of the electorate, according to major polls — both Democrats and Republicans must look to mobilize their rank-and-file supporters. To do so, the Republican Party has bet strongly this year on a strategy of convincing people that voter fraud is rampant.

As a scholar of U.S. politics, I see this as a high-risk strategy for Republican candidates and American democracy. That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can reduce motivation to vote – even if based on flawed information. But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November.

Voter fraud is not a real problem in the United States. Study after study, by public officials and think tanks, has shown that voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels.

Nonetheless, rhetoric from the Trump administration about voter fraud has been pervasive. Consider the recent claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls – a number reduced to 185 when state authorities pressed for details, and reduced to zero when the state investigated the names provided.

There is comparable behavior from Congress. My own research on political communication has shown that a substantial number of members of Congress, strongly skewing Republican, make frequent use of rhetoric that undermines democratic norms and delegitimizes political institutions.

The strategy ties readily into President Donald Trump’s persistent false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election. It also ties into his administration’s strongly anti-immigrant agenda, which spreads fear of noncitizens corrupting U.S. politics.
How does this uncertain political environment influence voters?

There is clear data showing that voter confidence in elections has fallen across party lines: Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable. Conventional wisdom suggests such discouraging numbers would depress turnout.
It’s not as simple as that, however.
Extensive research confirms the axiom that a sense of civic duty is the strongest predictor of whether someone will vote. It supersedes trust, partisanship and policy preferences.

Any campaign’s quest to mobilize additional voters, therefore, must find them among citizens without a strong sense of civic duty. But among these people, diminished trust in democratic processes can play out in counterintuitive ways.

Recent research on German voters is relevant to the U.S.: It shows that among more passive voters – those following cues from political elites – reduced trust in elections can depress motivation to vote. That’s because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm.
Conversely, among voters with greater skepticism about elite messaging, reduced trust can motivate increased turnout as an attempted corrective for a flawed system.
What does this mean for potential voters in the U.S.? Among Republicans, it appears that the party’s strategy carries a strong risk of backlash.

Findings from MIT’s Election Lab confirm that cues from political elites are a powerful factor in voter behavior. Specifically, cues setting expectations of a disappointing or untrustworthy result will reduce motivation. Why vote if you don’t expect it to help achieve the desired result?

The same study finds Republican voters broadly inclined to believe GOP leaders’ cues about voter fraud and to frame their expectations accordingly. And once they’ve made that shift, they cling firmly to the belief, even in the face of contrary empirical evidence or messaging from within the party.

In the current election cycle, 50% of Republicans surveyed distrust mail-in voting, and 51% fear voting by noncitizens. They expect election results to be fraudulent. This likely won’t mobilize them, as there’s no positive result they can expect to affirm. The Republican Party’s messaging has painted its voters into a corner.

Democrats, meanwhile, are less inclined to believe claims of voter fraud. But they are more inclined to be concerned about attempts to undermine the midterms by political elites making such claims. Examples include the Trump administration’s efforts to sow doubt about voting by mail and about alleged noncitizen voting.

These efforts increase motivation to vote among Democrats. Unlike GOP voters, they see the capacity to correct for the system’s vulnerabilities – the potential and urgency to overwhelm attempts at voter suppression through higher turnout.

Opponents of Trump and the GOP may find these diverging effects encouraging. No matter the results this November, however, we’re left with a precarious dynamic. Increasing numbers of voters lack trust in elections and make their decisions to vote – or not – based on limited or flawed information.
Fortunately, there are signs of hope.
Although voters in general are poorly informed about how elections are conducted, they can and do respond to clear information familiarizing them with election processes.

I’ve seen this myself over the years, working with nonpartisan efforts to register young adults and train them as poll watchers. And in the current election cycle, there have already been widespread efforts to broaden public awareness about the fact that state officials, not federal ones, have authority over voter rolls and election security.

Meanwhile, fewer Americans are expected to vote by mail this year – whether due to fear of fraud or fear of the Post Office. If they instead vote in person, a silver lining is that positive personal experiences with poll workers are also associated with increased voter trust.

Looking beyond November, what Americans can hope for is a cycle in which clear election outcomes provide an opportunity to inform voters of how and why the system works. That’s the way to motivate more political engagement and voter turnout in the future.

articles.title: Young voters fear mass shootings but are divided on gun control
articles.author: Jillian Turanovic, Professor of Sociology, University of Colorado Boulder
paras: An updated version of this article was published on Oct. 16, 2026. Read it here.

Nearly 50 million Americans ages 18 to 29 are eligible to vote in the upcoming midterm elections, and about 60% say they plan to. If they follow through, it would break midterm turnout records for voters under 30.

Gun control is an issue these young voters care about more than the public at large does, and it’s easy to understand why: In their lifetime, mass shootings have been a recurring part of American life.

Directly experiencing a mass shooting is rare, yet some young people have survived two before turning 25. When a gunman opened fire at Brown University in December 2025, at least two students on campus had already experienced a school shooting before they got to college. The same thing happened in April 2025, when students who lived through the 2018 Parkland, Florida, shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School found themselves caught in another shooting at Florida State University. As one of them put it: “This is America.”

Researchers have called today’s young adults the “massacre generation.” They’re the first group to grow up entirely in the post-9/11, post-Columbine High School shooting era, with routine lockdown drills, heightened security in schools and nonstop media coverage of mass violence.

As criminologists who study the impacts of victimization and gun violence among young people, we wanted to know how growing up with the threat of mass shootings has shaped young adults’ views on gun legislation. In a recent study, we surveyed nearly 1,700 young adults, ages 18 to 29, across the country to find out. We found that fear of mass shootings pulls this generation apart along political and gender lines: It pushes some toward wanting stricter gun laws and others in the opposite direction.
A debate that repeats after every shooting

Mass shootings account for about 1% of gun deaths in the U.S. Still, they profoundly shape how safe millions of Americans feel. In a 2019 survey by the American Psychological Association, nearly 80% of Americans said the possibility of a mass shooting stressed them out, and a third said they avoided certain places because of it. The fear has become so common that clinicians now have screening tools to assess and treat people with anxiety over mass violence.

Young adults have also grown up watching the same heated gun debates play out after every tragedy. Gun control advocates call for stricter firearm restrictions to prevent the next mass shooting, whereas gun rights advocates push back with the “good guy with a gun” argument, a phrase made popular by the National Rifle Association. Supporters of the latter view say more armed citizens are needed to stop active shooters, so more people should be able to buy and carry guns with fewer restrictions, such as carrying in public without a permit or on college campuses.

Researchers have known for a long time that more guns don’t necessarily mean less violence. A 2021 study found that mass shootings were more common in states with higher rates of gun ownership, and gun homicides were more common in states with looser concealed carry laws. Yet even after decades of mass shootings, federal gun policy has barely budged. Even where individual states and local governments have passed assault weapons bans, including Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois, they’ve faced Second Amendment challenges that are now before the Supreme Court.

Young people have become some of the loudest voices in this debate, most notably through March for Our Lives – an organization started by Parkland survivors that focuses on ending gun violence – and other youth-led groups across the country. And because pro-gun views tend to be more common among older Americans, many political observers assume stricter gun laws will follow as young people gain voting power.

This fall, voters will choose members of Congress and state lawmakers who can shape gun laws, and in a few states they’ll weigh in on gun policy directly. In Massachusetts, voters will decide whether to keep or repeal a 2024 law that, among other things, requires gun owners to register their firearms with the state, expands safety training for people applying for a gun license and broadens the state’s ban on assault-style weapons. In Arkansas, they’ll decide whether to change the state constitution to more strongly protect gun rights, including the right to own ammunition and gun parts. If young adults turn out in record numbers, their views could help determine outcomes like these.

So where do young adults stand? We’ve found that a shared fear of mass shootings does not necessarily lead to shared views on guns. Our survey asked young adults to rate on a scale from 1 to 3 – from “not at all” to “a lot” – how much they fear that they or someone they love will become a victim of a mass shooting. More than 60% reported moderate or high levels of fear, including about 17% who fell in the high-fear range.

In general, about two-thirds of young adults said people should need a permit to carry a gun in public and that guns shouldn’t be allowed on college campuses. About 6 in 10 disagreed that owning more guns makes people safer, and a similar share disagreed that gun control laws are unconstitutional.

We found that young adults who worried more about mass shootings tended to be more supportive of gun control. But this pattern didn’t hold for young men, Republicans or those who were politically conservative. For these groups, the opposite was true: The more they feared mass shootings, the less they supported gun restrictions. Young adults are divided on gun control, and those divisions are sharpest when fear runs high.

In the coming years, the massacre generation is on track to become part of the largest voting bloc in the country. Most young adults share a fear of mass shootings, but they disagree on what to do about them. And with each new mass shooting, that divide may only deepen.

articles.title: Can the Greens stick to their democratic principles?
articles.author: Mitya Pearson, Associate Professor, University of Warwick
paras: The Green Party of England and Wales’ prospects have fluctuated dramatically in recent years. At times, it has appeared on the cusp of becoming a major force at Westminster.
During this period, the Greens have had to balance their belief in internal party democracy while operating in a modern media and electoral environment.

Around the 2015 general election, the party’s membership and broader popularity surged, before the Labour Party picked Jeremy Corbyn as its leader and its subsequent move to the left stalled much of the Greens’ momentum.

Keir Starmer’s time as Labour leader allowed the Greens to once again successfully court progressive voters. They gained a record four MPs at the 2024 election, and their poll rating grew after Zack Polanski became leader in 2025.

But their popularity has slumped once again recently, something seemingly confirmed by their second-place finish in the recent Holborn and St Pancras byelection. They did, though, register their second-highest vote share in a byelection.

Over this period the Green Party of England and Wales and its sister parties in the rest of the UK have managed to consistently gain political representation at various levels, even if the Greens’ popularity and prominence have oscillated.
Dilution of democratic principles

Green parties are strongly associated with internal democracy. Many green parties have therefore had to manage this commitment once they have achieved national prominence and electoral success, at times leading to some dilution of democratic principles in the name of professionalisation. This was implied by Michels’ idea of the “iron law of oligarchy”: political parties tend towards hierarchical structures in the name of efficiency.

The Green Party of England and Wales is a pretty typical case. Historically, it had a strong, early commitment to the idea that it would not just seek to implement policies different from those of other parties, but approach politics in a distinct manner, including through participatory and democratic decision-making processes. There were numerous arguments over this within the Greens, reflecting the “fundi-realo” divide seen in Green parties in other countries.

In the early 1990s there were factious disputes over the “Green 2000” proposals for a more centralised organisational structure, with the reforms ultimately being adopted. Subsequently, a Rubicon was crossed in 2007 when the Greens voted to create the position of leader, replacing the previous shared principal speaker roles.

Nonetheless, the Greens have remained highly democratic compared to most other parties in the UK. Their policies are decided by votes at the party conference, which then provides the “foundation” for election manifestos and political programmes.

The Greens’ commitment to members deciding policy has created challenges for it as the party has become more prominent. At times members have voted for policies which have proved controversial, including the “Zionism is racism” motion which was recently passed at its conference. This has been widely criticised, with various Green figures distancing themselves from it.

The leader’s role is somewhat ambiguous as the party’s policy foundation is decided by conference votes and a leader may end up defending a position they may not agree with. Polanski said that he would have voted against the Zionism motion.

Journalists have often picked up on policies in areas such as migration, drugs and defence which have been agreed at Green conference, but can be awkward for party leaders to explain in media interviews. This is partly a product of the system where the party provides an underlying body of policy, but a different manifesto is put forward at elections.

The most likely route for the Greens to enter the UK government would be via a coalition. This is increasingly plausible given the British party system’s fragmentation. However, Westminster’s culture is not used to this type of arrangement and larger parties can face pressure to rule out working with controversial partners.

Indeed, Labour figures recently ruled out future cooperation with the Greens after the Zionism motion, and some Labour MPs even involved the police. Green leaders may also require their party members’ approval during any future coalition negotiations, which for most other UK party leaders would be unnecessary.

The Greens have, additionally, been grappling with practical issues. The party has grown, reaching over 200,000 members, meaning it is difficult for more than a small proportion of members to attend conferences and vote on policy.

There are reports that the current Green leadership has been looking at ways to amend its system of policymaking in light of its enlarged membership. Polanski has argued in the aftermath of the Zionism debate that “our party democracy must now evolve”. It seems very unlikely, however, that this will lead to a full-scale jettisoning of the party’s democratic structure.

Political parties’ roots and principles shape and constrain them, which means that they are often not totally free to make choices even if they consider them to be in their immediate tactical interest, and the Greens’ commitment to internal democracy runs very deep. None of the challenges which have been outlined here are necessarily insurmountable either.
Nonetheless, the Zionism motion has highlighted some of the tensions within a party, which is increasingly prominent in British politics, deciding its policy democratically.

articles.title: Why adoptive families can struggle to get help until they reach crisis point
articles.author: Claire Agius, Lecturer/Researcher, Manchester Metropolitan University
paras: In a deeply personal passage of his first Labour Party conference speech as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham paid tribute to the care workers who had looked after his father, Roy, who had Alzheimer’s disease and had died just two weeks earlier.

Those workers were “holding a threadbare system somehow together”, he said, yet remained “invisible to the political class of this country”. Addressing them directly, he added: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you.”

His words made me think about the care that goes unseen within families. Why are some forms of caring recognised as care, while others become almost invisible simply because they are considered part of family life?

I research trauma and adoption, and I am also an adoptive parent. I’m familiar with the story often told about adoption: a child finds a permanent family, a new life begins and everyone lives happily ever after.

But my research focuses on what happens after that supposed happy ending, particularly when the effects of a child’s earlier trauma continue into their adoptive family. And Burnham’s words made me wonder how much of the care provided by adoptive parents goes unrecognised simply because we call it parenting.
In England and Wales, an adoption order makes adopters the child’s legal parents. But a legal order cannot erase what happened beforehand.

Children adopted from care are often described as “previously looked-after”, a phrase I have long struggled with. There is nothing necessarily “previous” about the effects of their early experiences. A child may be physically safe but still struggle to feel safe. Earlier experiences can affect their development and their ability to trust the adults closest to them, since a family can be permanent in law long before a child feels secure enough to believe that permanence will last.

Adoptive parents are therefore living alongside the effects of experiences that happened before they even knew their child. This can make the parenting very different from what people usually imagine.

The relationship offering safety can also be the relationship in which fear and mistrust are expressed. For some families, this includes child-to-parent violence and abuse. A child experiencing overwhelming distress may run away or behave in ways that put themselves or others at risk. Parents may find themselves calling the police to protect their child or another family member, or because they fear for their own safety.

Understanding the reasons behind a child’s behaviour does not protect a parent from the emotional and physical impact of living with it. A parent can see why their child is hurting and still be hurt themselves.

My colleagues and I have researched compassion fatigue among adoptive parents raising children affected by early trauma. Compassion fatigue describes the emotional exhaustion and disconnection that can develop through repeated exposure to another person’s trauma.

My doctoral research also explored adoptive parents’ mental health more broadly. Parents described feeling exhausted while continuing to hold family life together. Sometimes, the very fact that they were managing made their distress harder for others to recognise.

The effects can reach beyond parents and children, affecting siblings and other family members. The adversity may belong to the child’s past, but its consequences can become part of the whole family’s present.
When families struggle to get help

Families are also affected by what happens outside the home. At school, a frightened child may be seen simply as badly behaved. A child who cannot get through the school gates may become an attendance problem. When the reasons behind their behaviour are overlooked, attention can quickly turn to what the parents are supposedly doing wrong.

Parents described fighting for help while feeling judged or blamed, sometimes until their family reached breaking point. Professionals, meanwhile, described recognising that families needed support but working within services that could not always provide it.

This is where Burnham’s description of a “threadbare system” particularly resonated with me. I have often described the services surrounding adoptive families as both traumatised and traumatising. Professionals are working under enormous pressure, often without the resources needed to respond to families’ complex needs. And when services are struggling, their responses can add to the distress of children and parents who are already finding life difficult.
For families, this can mean reaching a crisis and then having to demonstrate just how bad things have become before support is available.

Burnham’s words were powerful because they acknowledged care workers whose contribution is too often overlooked. But they also invite a wider conversation about what society recognises as care in the first place.

Care can come with a uniform and a job title. It can also mean a parent staying close to a child whose earliest relationships taught them that the adults they depend on may not always be safe or able to stay.
Helping a child learn to trust those relationships can take years, and the emotional demands on parents can be considerable. That work deserves recognition and support.
Care should not become less deserving of either simply because we call it parenting.

articles.title: What’s behind the BBC’s funding crisis? An expert explains
articles.author: Patrick Barwise, Emeritus Professor of Management and Marketing, London Business School
paras: In the run-up to the renewal of the BBC charter in January 2028, the corporation is facing perhaps its greatest ever funding crisis. It is staring down cost hyper-inflation across most programme genres and, unlike online-only streamers such as Netflix, it will still have to fund traditional broadcast networks until at least 2034. And of course, it will also have to pay for new digital services to keep pace with trends, especially among younger audiences.

But the biggest driver of the BBC crisis is the cut in real-terms funding for its national, regional and local UK services. These are the services that largely account for licence payers’ willingness to pay the fee.
The reduction in the real-terms funding of these services has been building up since 2010 and is now deeper than most people realise.

In 2010-11, TV licence fee revenue was £3.1 billion. The cost of collecting the licence fee was £124 million. The BBC also received £579 million of government funding from the Department for Work and Pensions for free TV licences for the over-75s.

So the total public funding from licence fees, after collection costs, and the DWP payment, was £3.5 billion. But not all of this went to the BBC: £80 million was “top-sliced” (or diverted) to meet the final costs of switching from analogue to digital TV.

By 2025-26, licence fee income had grown to £3.9 billion. But government support for free TV licences had been phased out and top-slicing increased to £293 million to fund the BBC World Service, BBC Monitoring (a division of the World Service), and the Local Democracy Reporting Service. The BBC was also partially funding the Welsh language TV channel S4C. That left the net public funding of its UK services at around £3.4 billion.

But between 2010 and 2025, the cumulative effect of inflation was 55.4%. This equates to a real-terms cut to public funding for the UK services of £2 billion per year – or put another way, a 37% drop in income.

Based on media coverage, you might think that the main reason for the BBC’s reduced income is that fewer people are paying the licence fee. But in reality, the 37% real-terms reduction was mainly driven by three other things.

First, successive governments were salami-slicing the value of the licence fee – in other words, repeated below-inflation settlements ate away at its value over time. Second, they withdrew government funding for free TV licences. Third, they more than doubled top-slicing in real terms, from £124 million to £293 million.
How BBC funding has fallen (figures in millions of pounds)

It’s true though that increases in licence fee evasion, from 5.2% in 2010-11 to 11.8% in 2025-26, played a part, as did the number of “no licence needed” households claiming that they did not need a TV licence because they “watch TV only on demand” but “never watch the BBC iPlayer”.

To put this into context, in 2015 99% of UK households used the BBC’s services in a single week. The figure may now be “only” 97% or 98%. But the idea that a large number are forced to pay without getting any direct benefit over a whole year seems implausible.
Many, however, take the BBC for granted – until they’re deprived of it. A study in 2022 found that after nine days without it, 70% of those who’d said it was poor value changed their minds.

To mitigate the cuts, the BBC has made continuous efficiency savings over the 15 years, reducing overhead costs, cutting staff and budgets, and squeezing suppliers. But, according to the National Audit Office, it now faces diminishing returns from these savings and most future cost-cutting will have to come from axed programmes, lower budgets and a reduction in the number of TV channels and radio stations. The axing of long-running Radio 4 consumer show You and Yours – along with other casualties – is a case in point.

The BBC also faces diminishing returns from commercial income, largely raised overseas from programme sales and format licences. With less investment in original content, quite simply the BBC now has less to sell.

The government says it wants to ensure sustainable BBC funding under the next charter. Achieving that will require updating or replacing the licence fee funding model, widening the payment base and bringing it closer to the BBC’s near-universal household usage. The financial stakes are surprisingly low: the £180 licence fee (with easy payment options) is equivalent to just £3.45 per week.

Limited, well-targeted exemptions for households for whom this is still a significant burden should be easily affordable, either for the government or for a properly funded BBC – even in the current fiscal situation. But as always, any policy that ends – or even reverses – the salami-slicing of BBC funding will be strongly opposed by its critics.

articles.title: Philly voters care about local issues, but election integrity fears make them wonder if their vote matters
articles.author: Heather LaMarre, Associate Professor of Media and Communication, Temple University
paras: Less than 30 days ahead of the 2026 midterms and almost nobody I talk to in Philadelphia is excited. Not my neighbors. Not my students or colleagues at Temple University, where I research and teach political communication and public opinion. Not even my politically engaged friends.
This mirrors the national mood in recent years: In a Pew Research Center survey, just 4% of Americans said they feel excited about politics; 65% said they feel exhausted.

“There are many factors that go into voter apathy,” explains Temple University political communications professor Bruce Hardy, “barriers to participation, lack of trust, cynicism, sense of disenfranchisement and powerlessness, political fatigue, and so on.”
Voter malaise and campaign fatigue aren’t new, but something feels different to me this time.

Lauren Cristella, president and CEO of the Committee of Seventy, a nonpartisan organization established to improve the voting process and engage Philadelphia citizens in the democratic process, agrees. She points to election integrity fears being hotly debated in the national media as part of the problem.

“We are sitting on the back side of a big decline in voter enthusiasm,” she said, “And yes, we need to start giving voters something to be excited about. However, what we are seeing in the commonwealth is a lot of confusion and fear around election integrity.”
This tension, in my view, is the real story of the 2026 midterms. Voters still care. The stakes are higher than ever. But the question on many voters’ minds is: Will my vote even count?
Election integrity fears are widespread

This is not just a Philadelphia problem. A July 2026 Gallup survey of more than 23,000 adults found that 2 in 3 Americans were concerned about political leaders pressuring election officials to change outcomes. Half worried that their own ballot would not be counted.
Voter confidence is sliding. In a 2026 University of California San Diego survey, 49% of Americans said they expect the midterms to be free and fair, while 51% expect unfair elections or aren’t sure.

A 2026 Pew survey similarly found that barely half of Americans are confident that November’s midterm elections will be conducted fairly and accurately. This represents a 10-point drop in national voter confidence from 61% in the 2024 elections.
Gap between democratic attitudes and voting behavior

Social and behavioral scientists have long understood the tension between one’s beliefs and attitudes about voting: For example, many people say they believe voting is an important democratic behavior, but then don’t actually vote themselves.

Efforts to close the gap between people’s intentions to vote and getting them to actually vote are where issues like mail-in voting, polling locations, time off work and voter ID laws make a difference.

Voting by mail has been a flash point since the 2020 presidential election when Philadelphia and Pennsylvania sat at the center of controversy. However, this should not be an issue for Philadelphians – or Pennsylvanians – in the upcoming midterms. The U.S. Supreme Court recently blocked a federal attempt to impose new Postal Service rules limiting mail-in voting.
Cristella told me that mail-in voting is “the safest and most secure of any time in the commonwealth’s history.” Every ballot can be tracked.
So why are Pennsylvania voters not convinced?
‘What’s the point?’ is a rational response

A 2021 article that cites experts at Tufts University explains how pushing myths like the “election was stolen” or “the election wasn’t fair” – presumably to explain away Donald Trump’s loss in 2020 and create mobilization for his 2024 presidential run – can boomerang and end up lowering confidence in future elections.

If people don’t believe their vote will count, then it becomes completely rational to simultaneously hold the opinion that voting is generally good for democracy, while also lacking any faith that their own vote will even be counted.
Framing theory explains how the presentation of information in the media influences the way people process and interpret it.

Hardy attributes much of the current state of voter apathy to the media’s focus on fraud and voter integrity. He says that “much of this comes from political discourse and media focusing on national political conflict, a seemingly endless election cycle, and a constant reinforcement of political in-groups and out-groups.”

Even though our elections are safe and secure in Philadelphia, he explains, “All of this negative national media coverage can overshadow the importance of local elections and leave people feeling disengaged from the politics closest to home.”
Cristella agrees that media framing is a significant part of the problem.

“Issues surrounding election fraud and vote integrity get amplified and muddied,” she said. When isolated issues in other states occur, even if proved untrue, the intense and repeated national media attention on them shakes voter confidence here at home.
What this means for Philly

The 2026 midterms will be an important election for Pennsylvania, as the election will determine the state’s next governor and lieutenant governor, as well as members of the U.S. House of Representatives and the state Legislature.
Philadelphians have a lot on the line.

Economic concerns, in particular, are a major issue this election. A recent Gallup poll indicates that confidence in the economy is at its weakest level since 2022. And the voters are feeling the pinch.
While the 2026 Philadelphia primary had a low 22% turnout, Cristella believes issues like affordability will lead to a strong turnout in November.
As a longtime Philadelphian who believes strongly in our democracy, I am staying hopeful.
Pennsylvania has 40,000 poll workers for each election. To become a poll worker, visit vote.phila.gov or vote.pa.gov.

articles.title: Republicans can confirm a Supreme Court justice if Democrats take the Senate, but at what cost?
articles.author: Paul M. Collins Jr., Professor of Legal Studies and Political Science, UMass Amherst
paras: Democrats are gaining momentum in their bid to retake the Senate in November. This has led Republicans to prepare for the possibility that a conservative Supreme Court justice might announce their retirement before the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027.
This would give President Donald Trump his fourth Supreme Court nomination, helping to ensure conservative dominance on the court for decades.

As a Supreme Court scholar, I know that judicial appointments have real consequences. Look no further than Roe v. Wade: Within two years of securing a 6–3 conservative majority, the high court in 2022 eliminated the constitutional right to abortion that had existed for almost 50 years.
If Democrats take over the Senate and a Republican-appointed justice retires before Jan. 3, this will trigger one of the most explosive confirmation battles in American history.
Here’s how the fight is likely to play out – and why the stakes are so high.
Who is most likely to retire?

Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas top the list of potential retirees should Democrats win the Senate in November. Alito and Thomas are the court’s oldest justices, at 76 and 78, respectively. Thomas is also the court’s longest-serving justice, appointed by President George H.W. Bush in 1991.

Perhaps more importantly, both justices have deep ties to the conservative legal movement. This is a network of lawyers, judges and politicians who seek to etch conservative principles into law. Overturning Roe v. Wade was at the top of the conservative wish list.
My research suggests that both Alito and Thomas care about their legacies. And they both understand that a Democratic-controlled Senate would block another Trump-appointed nominee.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer made this clear on Oct. 5, 2026, as did Senate Judiciary Committee member Richard Blumenthal, the Democrat from Connecticut. Blumenthal said, “It is slim to none that we would support a nominee from this administration.”

Though Alito has recently indicated he intends to stay on the court through its 2026 term, Thomas has made no recent public statements about retirement. And Alito is free to change his mind at any time.

If Alito or Thomas announced their retirement after the midterms, Republicans would have enough time to confirm a successor. The Senate has four and a half work weeks scheduled between Election Day and Jan. 3. Justice Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed less than a month after her nomination, making the timeline tight but doable.

Democrats will likely attempt to slow down the process, but they face an uphill battle with few options. Republicans stripped away key delaying tactics in recent years by ending the filibuster in 2017 and ignoring the Judiciary Committee’s quorum rules in 2020. This rule requires nine members be present to transact business, including two members of the minority party.
A potentially historic battle
A Republican effort to confirm a Supreme Court nominee during a lame-duck Senate would spark a historic battle with Democrats.

Democrats would surely point to how Republicans handled President Barack Obama’s appointment of Merrick Garland in 2016. A seat on the court opened up after conservative Antonin Scalia died on Feb. 13, almost nine months before the November presidential election.

Republicans refused to move Garland’s nomination through the confirmation process, using their majority power to set the Senate’s agenda. This marked the first time since 1866 that a Supreme Court nomination that was not withdrawn failed to receive an up-or-down vote in the Senate.

To justify this, Republicans created the so-called “McConnell Rule,” named after former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky. According to McConnell, the Senate should not fill Supreme Court vacancies “in the middle of a presidential election year.”
Four years later, Senate Republicans abruptly abandoned the rule. This allowed them to push through Coney Barrett’s confirmation just days before the 2020 presidential election.
Democrats did not take kindly to this reversal.
Schumer pulled no punches in a speech the day of Barrett’s confirmation vote. Schumer said the day “will go down as one of the darkest days in the 231-year history of the United States Senate.”

He alleged the Republican majority made “a mockery of its own stated principle – that the American people deserve a voice in the selection of Supreme Court Justices – completing the partisan theft of two seats on the Supreme Court using completely contradictory rationales.”
Democrats were clearly outraged by what they saw as two stolen Supreme Court seats.
However, I believe that pushing through a nominee will trigger an even fiercer fight. Senate Democrats will see such a confirmation as a power grab that sidelines the voice of voters.
Furthermore, if a Republican justice retires should Democrats win the Senate, the move will almost certainly be viewed as purely partisan.

This has the potential to further erode public support for the court, which is sitting near historic lows. And it will likely fuel the fire of Supreme Court reform, including the possibility of expanding the number of justices on the court.
Put simply, in securing a short-term conservative victory, Republicans may end up handing Democrats the exact justification they need to reshape the high court.

articles.title: In newly independent US, Americans debated whether public executions taught a lesson or just showed off the state’s power to destroy
articles.author: Maurizio Valsania, Professor of American History, Università di Torino
paras: The proposed livestream of Nidal Hasan’s execution by a U.S. military firing squad gave an old question a new audience. Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted by a military court of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3, 2026.
Explaining the plan to make his death public, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said that “people need to understand … there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”

But on Oct. 15, 2026, President Donald Trump announced in a social media post that Hasan’s execution would not be livestreamed, after the plan drew widespread public objections from both Republicans and Democrats.

In his Truth Social post canceling the livestream, Trump wrote “I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan.” And as a historian of the early American republic, I recognize that familiar expectation: that watching someone die will teach a useful lesson. Americans at the republic’s founding debated that premise – and doubted what the lesson might be.
On Aug. 17, 1797, New Yorkers gathered to watch John Young hang.
An English musician and music publisher struggling with debt, Young had shot and killed Robert Barwick, a deputy sheriff taking him into custody. Barwick left a widow and nine children.
Young’s conviction by a jury brought him to a scaffold surrounded by soldiers, before an immense crowd.

Governor John Jay, a leading Federalist who placed greater faith in firm government than in popular judgment, had authorized the military presence after the sheriff reported fears of a rescue. But Jay also wanted the execution to impress its witnesses with the power of the government carrying it out.

Writing to James Kent, New York City’s chief municipal legal officer, two days before the hanging, Jay stressed that the authority of law should prevail visibly. The occasion should be “particularly solemn and impressive,” he said. The “authority of the law should be seen to bear down (on) all opposition.”

Solemnity, however, proved difficult to arrange. The military escort played lively music as the procession made its way to the scaffold. One newspaper critic thought an uninformed passerby might mistake the spectacle for “the celebration of some Festival.”

Soldiers formed a square around the gallows. The crowd remained orderly. Young addressed a few words to the minister, sang a psalm “and with great composure pulled his cap over his face,” reported one newspaper. Then, before the assembled witnesses, he was hanged.
Loss of government’s dignity
Whatever the crowd’s reaction that day, the public execution had already become an argument about the nature of government.

The display did not impress everyone as evidence of governmental strength. Writing in the “Greenleaf’s New York Journal” two weeks after the hanging, “A CITIZEN” accused Jay of “letting down the dignity of civil authority.” Calling out troops for the execution suggested, among other things, “a wantonness on the part of the Executive.”
To this critic, the military presence advertised executive excess. The spectacle could undermine the very authority it was meant to affirm.
That point mattered in a republic still deciding how its authority should differ from that of the European monarchies that Americans portrayed as corrupt.
In the 1780s and 1790s, American reformers took particular aim at England’s “sanguinary laws” – statutes prescribing death for offenses ranging from murder to relatively minor theft.

By 1776, nearly 200 offenses carried a possible death sentence in England. These laws had accumulated piecemeal over generations, but American critics portrayed them as a single system with bloodshed at its center.

England’s punishments became a measure of what republican justice must overcome. Independence required Americans to reconsider how readily, and under what circumstances, their own governments could take a life.

The contrast was partly an exercise in national self-definition. Americans cast English severity as evidence of an old, corrupt political order and imagined their own laws as rational, proportionate and suited to free citizens.
In practice, the distinction was harder to sustain.

Nevertheless, the aspiration entered constitutional language. New Hampshire’s 1784 Constitution declared a multitude of sanguinary laws “both impolitic and unjust.” Punishment’s proper object was “to reform, not to exterminate mankind.”
Reform did not necessarily mean abolition. In 1796, New York reduced the number of crimes punishable by death but retained capital punishment for murder.
Young went to the gallows the following year. Even if Jay favored milder criminal laws, he was able to see a carefully staged execution as a necessary assertion of public authority.
No guarantee of lesson learned
Other Americans pressed further.

Benjamin Rush, the Philadelphia physician and signer of the Declaration of Independence, opposed executing even murderers. His argument went to the heart of the relationship between government and the governed.
“Capital punishments are the natural offspring of monarchical governments,” Rush wrote in 1792. “Kings consider their subjects as their property.”

For Rush, a republic that put citizens to death still acted like a monarchy, treating citizens’ lives as its own to dispose of. Calling the killing a lawful punishment did not make it less an act of revenge.
A related debate concerned the audience. Even Americans who accepted capital punishment could doubt the wisdom of making it public.

In 1787, Rush had already questioned what spectators actually learned from watching others suffer. Sympathy for the condemned could turn them against the government: “We secretly condemn the law which inflicts the punishment – hence arises a want of respect for laws in general,” he wrote in a pamphlet titled “An Enquiry into the Effects of Public Punishments upon Criminals and upon Society.”

Alternatively, repeated exposure to cruelty could harden spectators, encouraging the very violence that punishment was supposed to deter. “How often,” Rush asked, “do we find pockets picked under a gallows, and highway-robberies committed within sight of a gibbet?”

The crowd could pity the condemned, admire his composure or simply enjoy an outing. Gathering witnesses did not guarantee that they absorbed the intended lesson. The complaint about festive music at Young’s execution exposed that uncertainty: Officials could stage the spectacle, but they could not control its meaning.
What harm does this prevent?

Young’s execution gives the proposed broadcast of Hasan’s death a particular resonance. The crimes, jurisdictions and audiences differ, yet the ambition remains recognizable: to make one person’s punishment teach everyone else a lesson – and demonstrate the government’s strength.

Cruelty concerns more than the pain inflicted. It also lies in treating a person as fodder for exposure, humiliation and public instruction. The condemned person’s body becomes a public demonstration of whom the state protects – and whom it has the power to destroy.

But spectators may come for the theater of death itself, drawn by fascination with what human beings can do to one another. What officials present as instruction can become the marketing of guilty pleasures.

Cesare Beccaria, an Italian criminologist and economist whose 1764 essay “On Crimes and Punishments” helped shape American reform debates, argued that punishment could not undo a crime, only prevent future harm. Suffering beyond that purpose was unnecessary cruelty.

For Beccaria, an execution’s fleeting spectacle deterred less effectively than lifelong penal servitude. Beccaria’s alternative was harsh, but his principle constrained the state: The power to inflict suffering did not establish its necessity.

At Young’s scaffold, the state could end his life without controlling the meaning of his death. A broadcast would vastly enlarge the audience, but reach is no proof of usefulness, and curiosity supplies no justification.
Beccaria’s question thus remains: What future harm does this additional spectacle prevent? If it prevents none, what justifies it – and what does it reveal about the government that stages it?
This story was updated on Oct. 15, 2026, to reflect the cancellation of the livestream of Hasan’s execution.

articles.title: How Trump’s disaster aid delays and FEMA cuts could galvanize the ‘movable middle’ in the 2026 elections
articles.author: Dana R. Fisher, Director of the Center for Environment, Community & Equity and Professor in the School of International Service, American University School of International Service
paras: When Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle on Oct. 9, 2026, it was just the latest weather disaster for Americans in a year that continues to break records.

The hottest U.S. summer on record left millions of Americans facing life-threatening heat waves. Extreme heat and drought set the stage for wildfires. Flooding from powerful storms and days of heavy rainfall inundated communities in several states. And now a “Super El Niño,” on top of already rising temperatures and sea levels, is expected to make extreme events worse, at least into spring 2027.

In the past, states relied heavily on federal aid and expertise to respond quickly to disasters. But in communities across the U.S., people recovering from floods, storms and wildfires in 2025 and 2026 have been left waiting much longer for federal aid – if it arrives at all.
Will there be political consequences in the midterm elections for the slow aid and lack of government assistance?

The answer to that question runs through the ways the Trump administration has changed disaster response and federal disaster aid. As a professor who has written for years about civic engagement and climate policy, I have reason to believe that voters’ frustration with slow disaster aid may show up at the polls.
Cuts to FEMA hobbled federal disaster help
Even though the United States is experiencing more disasters as the climate changes, the federal programs meant to help Americans recover are being diminished.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency has faced significant cuts to funding and staff since the Trump administration took office in January 2025. The administration initially talked about abolishing the agency, arguing that states and communities could deal with disasters on their own. It created a plan to cut FEMA’s staffing by 50%, but in September 2026, a judge found that plan to be unlawful.

FEMA lost over 17% of its trained staff members in 2025 alone, including hundreds of people who were on call to respond to disasters. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to defend the administration’s goal of a leaner workforce at the agency.

The Trump administration also withheld billions of dollars meant to help states reduce their disaster risk and protect homes, hospitals and other structures from storm damage. Lawsuits forced the administration to restore some of the funds, but many communities are still struggling on their own.
These changes have tangible effects on how well states are able to recover from disasters and how well they can prepare for the disaster risks ahead as the climate changes.
Slower aid, if it arrives at all
The Trump administration is also taking longer to approve emergency funding after disasters than past administrations did and denying more of those requests.
In 2025 it denied 26% of requests for major disaster declarations, which unlock immediate federal aid. That was up from an average of 15% over the previous two decades.

An independent analysis of FEMA data exposes some clear patterns in funding delays under the Trump administration. The review found that major disaster declarations have taken an average of nearly 10 weeks to be issued during the current Trump administration, up from an average of three weeks or less over the previous two decades.

The administration says it is simply conducting more thorough reviews when governors make these aid requests. But people caught in disasters don’t have time to wait. Major disaster aid includes individual assistance, such as temporary housing, loans and repair grants, that disaster survivors need quickly to recover.

The review also found that about 85% of the requests for federal assistance from states that went for Donald Trump in the 2024 election were eventually approved, while only about half of requests have been approved in states that voted for his Democratic opponent, Kamala Harris.

A separate Associated Press report in July 2026 noted that no other president had such a sharp partisan divide in approving disaster declaration requests between Republican and Democratic governors since at least 1989, when a federal law set rules for disaster determinations.
Disaster failures can mobilize political moderates
A handful of studies, including mine, have found that people who have experienced a disaster often have higher levels of civic engagement.

In my study, civic engagement included contacting elected officials, signing petitions, attending public meetings, participating in boycotts or joining protests, among other actions. We didn’t look at the connection to voting patterns, but I believe there is good reason to expect our findings to extend to voting as well.

The relationship between experiencing a disaster and level of civic engagement was strongest for political moderates who are sometimes referred to as the “movable middle” – they could swing in either political direction if they have reason to do so.

Given the disasters America has seen in recent years and the sharp drop in federal assistance, I expect that political moderates who become more civically engaged will play a significant role in the midterm elections this year.
How FEMA cuts play out in a crisis
Several recent disasters have shown what happens when the federal government isn’t prepared to respond quickly.

After the devastating July 4 floods that swept through Texas Hill Country in 2025, the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees FEMA, waited three days before approving funding to send federal search-and-rescue teams, a Congressional report confirmed. Other funding approvals took an average of 12 days, leaving local and state programs to fill critical gaps in disaster systems.
In summer 2026, Texas was hit with floods again. The president approved assistance for some of the counties after a seven-week delay. Other requests for assistance were still waiting months later.
FEMA denied individual and statewide assistance to Michigan after severe storms and tornadoes tore up homes across several rural communities in March 2026.

With highly contested Senate races looming in both states, these actions by the Trump administration could color voters’ views or contribute to a lack of enthusiasm for the party in power and even increase support for the opposition.

A survey conducted by Pew Research Center in May 2025 found that the majority of Americans believe that it is a good idea for the federal government to provide financial assistance to help people rebuild after disasters in place at high risk of extreme weather.

These findings are relatively consistent across political parties: 60% of those who identified as Republican or leaning Republican said they believed it was a good idea, as did 68% of those who identified as Democrat or leaning Democrat.

Trump recently started announcing disaster aid approvals in states consequential to the control of Congress in the midterm elections, including in Wisconsin and Ohio. In some cases, he coupled his candidate endorsements with disaster funding announcements.
I don’t believe those late announcements will move the needle in his party’s favor at this late date.

articles.title: I’ve been studying election integrity for 26 years, and here’s why I expect a normal election this November instead of chaos
articles.author: Justin Levitt, Professor of Law, Loyola Law School Los Angeles
paras: Fear of federal interference in the 2026 midterms, from intimidation stoked by armed officials at the polls to seizure of ballots, has been growing in the United States. That’s led state and local voting officials across the country to draw up plans for scenarios requiring them to summon law enforcement or prepare legal filings so they can keep the polls open.

In an interview with The Conversation’s politics and legal affairs editor Naomi Schalit, election law scholar Justin Levitt takes the temperature down a bit. Levitt says that while voting officials’ preparations mean they are doing their jobs, the anticipated election interference won’t happen – in part because of that preparation.
Schalit: Could we see widespread intimidation and challenging of voters at the polls?

Levitt: It’s extremely unlikely. I completely understand that Americans are freaked out. They are at an electric level of anxiety right now, not just about the world but about the coming elections. But I don’t think the intimidation and challenges they’re fearing or forecasting are going to manifest for a couple reasons.

I have run a nationwide election protection program. It’s real work to get people to dedicate a full day to helping others. It’s that much harder to recruit a group of people to show up and look for fraud, and fraud at scale doesn’t really happen. It’s even harder to recruit people to show up to actively intimidate voters.

Not that many people are in for it – there are keyboard warriors who love to act out online, but to actually show up is a totally different thing. And they’re really risking either getting thrown out of the polling place or going to jail, because intimidating voters is a crime.
What about intimidation and challenges by government officials?

On the government side, which is something people are also really freaked out about, we are a giant country and there are almost 100,000 polling places. The logistics of an intimidation operation don’t work countrywide.
To go from Step A, I’d like to intimidate people, to Step C, intimidate people everywhere? You’re missing a pretty giant Step B.

Here’s what I believe will happen: The federal government will send a group of a dozen goons to a suburban polling place somewhere, and they’ll have a camera crew with them. Bystanders will happily oblige them in filming. That clip will go viral and scare voters into not showing up at the polls because they think that there are individuals intimidating voters all over the place.
If people are worried about intimidation, go outside and see for yourself that in your neighborhood things are very normal. Even if social media depicts pure chaos.
Local and state election officials are preparing for mayhem or interference by the federal government. Are their efforts just based on overwrought imaginations?

No, they are being responsible. It’s their responsibility to prepare for everything so that the voters don’t have to worry about it. And they are as prepared as I have ever seen them. They’re preparing for a lot of truly outlandish scenarios, and some that are more realistic, so that they can be ready to make sure that the election is smooth and secure and feels very normal.
Could ballots be seized by state or federal officials?

Ballot seizure is also very much on people’s minds, and I think it’s particularly salient because the feds did it in Fulton County, Georgia, and because local sheriffs did it in Riverside, California. But there are two big reasons that’s not going to happen this fall.

First, the seizures in both Fulton County and Riverside were of old ballots. Fulton County’s ballots were 6 years old. California was more recent. It was a 2026 seizure for the 2025 elections, but those elections were still over and results had already been tallied.

That’s very different from an attempt to seize ballots while results are still pending, which is flatly unconstitutional. I just worked on an article with the former chief of the public integrity section at the U.S. Department of Justice. We did a lot of research and we think there’s never before been a federal warrant to seize ballot material when the results are pending. And that’s because judges don’t like to sign off on things that are illegal.

These seizures, in Fulton County and in Riverside, California, surely took the judges in those districts by surprise. Judges see applications for search warrants all the time, all day, every day. But warrants for election materials when the results are still pending are vanishingly rare. The warrants in Fulton and Riverside did us a favor because there are very few judges anywhere who are going to be surprised right now. Those seizures were big news.

In Fulton County, the judge allowed it, but he said very, very clearly this would be different if we were talking about a pending election where results weren’t still in the door. In California, the trial judge signed off on it. But the California Supreme Court came back just about a month ago, said this was absolutely, flatly illegal, there is absolutely no reason why a sheriff needs to seize these ballots. It is unlawful under California state law in a way that mimics other states’ laws too.

If somehow ballots get seized during the election process before they are counted and certified, that would mean that the chain of custody was broken and they would no longer be valid. Is that correct?

In the extraordinarily unlikely event that there’s actually a seizure, we’re in a little bit of terra incognita. It’s not entirely clear what happens. There will be immediate efforts legally to get the ballots back.

But the election system is built with belts and suspenders. If there’s a seizure of some materials, that doesn’t mean there’s a seizure of all materials or all materials relevant to a count. Sometimes there are paper ballots that are backed up by electronic copies, or vice versa. So what’s really important is that the election officials have a set of reliable records they can count.

The federal government may come in and say, “Give us the materials,” and the states are likely to say, “How about we make you copies?” And that’s fine. They can go off and have their copies and do whatever they want with them as long as the states are still able to count the records. It’s not really clear what would happen if there’s an extended lapse where the ballots are out of state custody. It’s not that those ballots are immediately invalid, but there’d be a fight about it.

I’ve been covering politics for a long time, and in the past 10 years the number of times we’ve gone into terra incognita was entirely unanticipated. Which is why I have to ask certain questions that seem completely implausible.

I’ve been working on elections for a couple decades now. My list of things to watch out for in 2000 was long. My list of things to watch out for in every subsequent election grew longer. The last couple of years, my list of things to watch out for has spilled off the page and onto the floor. For election officials, it’s a lot. They are stressed out, they’re underpaid, they’re overworked.
But all that said, they’ve got this. They’re actually as prepared as I have ever seen, including dealing with things that they haven’t ever seen before and should never have to be seeing.

I understand why people are afraid. I understand why people think there are risks. And that’s because it’s not normal to have the president fostering this much concern about the democratic process and who is this unattached to the democratic process.
But the good news is the process doesn’t depend on the president. It depends on us.
